query: how to choose an ai agent builder
title: How to choose an AI agent builder: 8 questions | 50agents
description: Choose an AI agent builder by testing one real job: does it reach your apps, ask before it acts, show what it did, and cost what you expect?
h1: How to choose an AI agent builder
answer: Take one real job, build it in two or three builders on their free tiers, and compare them on eight questions, from whether it reaches your apps and asks before risky actions to what one run costs and whether you can leave.
Feature lists matter less than how the tool behaves on your job.

head: Question
What a good answer looks like
rows: Your apps, and the specific actions the job needs, are in its catalog.
2. Can I limit what each AI agent touches?
Per-agent apps and accounts, not one key for everything.
3. Does it ask before risky actions?
Sends, payments and deletions wait for a person, enforced by the product.
4. Can I see what it did?
Each run with what it read, what it decided and what it changed.
A clear unit (credits, tasks, runs) and the cost of your job’s run shown after testing.
Change it in words or in a form; a version history with undo.
Export your data and instructions; no lock-in to one model.
A company with a track record. Relay.app, often recommended in these lists, says on its own site that it has shut down.

body.p: Glean’s guide weights capabilities 25%, integrations 20%, security 20%, ease 15%, vendor 10% and cost 10%. For a small team we would move cost and ease up: an AI agent you cannot afford to run daily, or cannot fix yourself, does not get used. For how builders charge, see [how much automation costs](/guides/how-much-automation-costs-credits-tasks-and-runs-compared).

method.h2: How to run the test, step by step

steps.title: Pick one real job
steps.body: One you do weekly, with real apps and a send at the end. "Follow up quiet deals" is a good test.

steps.title: Shortlist two or three builders
steps.body: By question 1: they must reach your apps.

steps.title: Build it in each on the free tier
steps.body: Time how long it takes and note where you got stuck.

steps.title: Run each on the same 10 real cases
steps.body: Compare the outputs side by side. Count edits needed.

steps.title: Check the run log and the bill
steps.body: Can you see why it did what it did? What did the 10 runs cost?

steps.title: Break it on purpose
steps.body: Disconnect an app, feed it an odd case. See what it tells you.

body: In 50agents you start the test with one sentence. Captain shows the plan with the apps it uses and what asks you first before anything is built, the AI agent’s runs and their receipts are on its page and in Activity, so you can see what it read and why it did what it did.

wrong.title: Choosing from a feature list
wrong.body: Every list says "integrations" and "memory". Only a real job shows the difference.

wrong.title: Costs you cannot predict
wrong.body: Usage per run varies with what the AI agent reads. Run your job 10 times and look at the bill before scheduling it.

wrong.title: An AI agent stuck in a loop
wrong.body: It retries and spends. Prefer builders that cap runs and show failed runs plainly.

wrong.title: Weak logs
wrong.body: You cannot explain to a customer why they got an email. Make question 4 a hard requirement.

wrong.title: The vendor goes away
wrong.body: It happens. Keep your instructions and data exportable.

faqs.q: What is the best no-code AI agent builder?
faqs.a: The one that runs your real job well, in your apps, at a cost you accept. Test two or three on the same job rather than trusting rankings.

faqs.q: AI agent builder or automation tool?
faqs.a: An automation tool for fixed steps; an AI agent builder when each case needs judgement. Many jobs need a bit of both. See [AI agent vs automation](/guides/ai-agent-vs-automation-which-one-you-need).

faqs.q: How much do AI agents cost to run?
faqs.a: From a fraction of a cent to a few cents a run for small jobs, more for AI agents that read a lot. Builders price in credits, so test your job and read the usage log.
